catalog_quote: In addition, Puxian is a tone language, which is noteworthy for complex tone sandhi phenomena. There are 7 tones, as shown in Table 3. ... Tone sandhi occurs when two monosyllabic lexemes join together. There are about 49 tone sandhi combinations used in daily speech (Cai Guomei 2006: 14). The tone of the first lexeme changes according to that of the second, whereas the tone of the second lexeme remains basically the same. For instance, the tone value Ying Ping 533 will change to Yang Qu 11, when it meets with another Ying Ping 533, as in the case of hi533 ‘fly’ to hi11-ki533 ‘fly-machine’ or ‘plane’ || (p. 18:) In the majority of cases, each morpheme has a ‘combination tone’ (a tone occurs in combination with the following full tone, e.g. sandhi tone) or an ‘isolation tone’ (a tone that occurs in isolation or is followed by an unstressed tone).

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (376 pp., the PDF's metadata gives the title "The Function of Pronominal Expressions") and re-extracted PDF pp. 17-25 with extracted text. All three quoted passages are present verbatim: (a) PDF p. 24 = printed p. 22, end of §1.4.1 Phonology: "In addition, Puxian is a tone language, which is noteworthy for complex tone sandhi phenomena. There are 7 tones, as shown in Table 3."; (b) the continuation "Tone sandhi occurs when two monosyllabic lexemes join together. There are about 49 tone sandhi combinations used in daily speech (Cai Guomei 2006: 14). The tone of the first lexeme changes according to that of the second, whereas the tone of the second lexeme remains basically the same."…
new_statements.rule_in_words: No rule for word-stress placement is given by any description opened. Puxian is described purely as a tone language: seven lexical tones (Putian 533, 13, 453, 42, 11, 21, 4), with two-syllable tone sandhi in which the first syllable changes and the second keeps its citation tone; the second syllable's initial undergoes mutation. Wu's only reference to stress is that a morpheme keeps its isolation tone when 'followed by an unstressed tone', i.e. neutral-tone/unstressed syllables exist, but which syllables they are is not stated.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated for stress. For tone: 阳入 has an old-style colloquial 35 reading merging with 阳平 (莆田市志 F06; 方言志); Xianyou values differ from Putian.
new_statements.domain_note: Statements concern lexical tone on isolated syllables and sandhi in two-syllable compounds/phrases (词/词组); no phrase-level prominence or citation-form stress is discussed. The gazetteers 莆田市志 2001 (卷四十三 方言, all 97 page images scanned-searched) and 福建省志·方言志 1998 (第三章 莆仙方言, sandhi text + tables) and the instrumental thesis Chen 2014 are entirely silent on 轻声/重音/stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Wu 2010's corpus was recorded in Licheng (鲤城), the county seat of Xianyou (仙游), the author's native town, while his phonology table follows Putian-based descriptions (Cai 2006; Putian tone values 533/24/453/42/11/21/4). Chen 2014 describes Putian city (莆田市区) speech; Chen Hong 2018 describes Xianyou county; the gazetteers take 莆田城关话 as representative and give Xianyou values alongside. Glottolog puxi1243 has no separate codes for the Putian and Xianyou dialects, so all of these fall under puxi1243.

sources.locator: §1.4.1 Phonology, p. 22 (PDF p. 24); transcription conventions §1.3, p. 18 (PDF p. 20)
sources.note: Sketch 1.4.1 Phonology (pp. 20-23): 15 consonants, 39 rimes, 7 tones (values from Cai 2006), ~49 two-syllable sandhi combinations where the first syllable changes and the second keeps its tone; 'Puxian is a tone language, which is noteworthy for complex tone sandhi phenomena' (p. 22). The only reference to stress is a parenthetical in the transcription conventions (p. 18): an 'isolation tone' is 'a tone that occurs in isolation or is followed by an unstressed tone'. No rule for stress placement.

sources.note: Acoustic description of Putian-city speech: 15 onsets, 45 rimes, 7 citation tones (T1a 54, T1b 35, T2 443, T3a 52, T3b 22, T4a 2, T4b 4), phonation contrasts. Not a word on stress, accent or neutral tone.
Only Wu 2010 as descriptive reference (plus Kwok 2024 subclassification comment, Eberhard et al. 2025). No dialect-level glottocodes for Putian / Xianyou.
